basics.name: KMODDL (Kinematic Models for Design Digital Library), Cornell University Library
basics.url: https://engineering.library.cornell.edu/kmoddl/ (current landing page; the old address https://kmoddl.library.cornell.edu/ redirects here). It points to three places: the image and GIF collection on Cornell University Library Digital Collections (https://digital.library.cornell.edu/collections/kmoddl, which is bot-protected and could not be opened from here), the historic texts on eCommons (https://ecommons.cornell.edu/handle/1813/57656), and the original 2003 site archived on Archive-It
basics.resource_type: digital library (photos, animated GIFs, videos and simulations of Cornell's Reuleaux kinematic model collection, plus digitised historic books, now spread across library platforms)
basics.license: Described as 'open access', but the landing page gives no single licence. eCommons items show no licence field in their metadata. Search-result snippets for Digital Collections item pages suggest the rights are mixed: Jon Reis's photographs are licensed to Cornell for educational display only, while other items are under CC BY 4.0. These pages could not be opened to confirm [uncertain]. What this means for the encyclopedia: link to it freely, and only reuse an image after checking that item's own rights statement
basics.language: English (the site and descriptions). Some digitised historic texts are in German, French or Latin (e.g. Voigt's 1907 'Kinematische Modelle nach Prof Reuleaux', Huygens' 'Horologium oscillatorium')
basics.year: Original site released 2003, funded by an NSF National Science Digital Library (NSDL) grant for 2002-2004 and an IMLS library-museum grant for 2004-2006. Image metadata credits creation to 2002-2006 [uncertain]. The original site has since been archived, and its content moved to Cornell Library Digital Collections and eCommons. The landing page is live in 2026, but no new models appear to have been added since the grant period [uncertain]
basics.access_barrier: none (open access; no login). Note: Cornell's Digital Collections site uses a browser bot-check, which normal browsers pass
basics.image_license: Mixed per item: professional photos (Jon Reis Photography) are licensed to Cornell for educational display only (not openly reusable), while some other images, GIFs and videos are reported as CC BY 4.0 [uncertain]. The 19th-century models themselves are public-domain designs, so new photos you take or 3D models you draw of them are not restricted by KMODDL
basics.authority_level: academic (Cornell University Library with Cornell Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering and Mathematics faculty, e.g. Francis C. Moon and Hod Lipson; the collection is an ASME Mechanical Engineering Heritage Collection. Descriptions are curated rather than peer-reviewed)

coverage.covers: Cornell's Reuleaux collection of 19th-century teaching models of machine elements (about 220 Voigt-catalogue Reuleaux models; ASME counts 230 Reuleaux models among about 300 artifacts), plus about a dozen Schroeder models and a Willis model. The models cover lower and higher pairs, crank and slider linkages, gear teeth, planetary gear trains, ratchets and indexing (step) mechanisms, clock escapements, universal joints and couplings, belt drives and belt shifters, friction wheels, reversing gears, rotary pumps (capsular mechanisms), straight-line and parallel-motion linkages, cams and curves of constant width (the Reuleaux triangle). eCommons holds 58 reference items: digitised historic machine books ('theatres of machines' such as Bockler, Ramelli and Leupold), Voigt's catalogue of Reuleaux models, Reuleaux biographies and papers about the project. The 2005 descriptions also list tutorials for middle-school to undergraduate level, mathematical simulations and STL files for 3D-printing working replicas
coverage.organisation: Originally a website with one page per model (description, history, photos, movies, simulations). Now it is a Digital Collections search portal with faceted browsing (by agent/maker, subject and so on) and a canned search for animated GIFs, plus a separate eCommons list of texts. Models are identified by the Voigt catalogue code (a letter for the class plus a number, e.g. S35) [uncertain]. For beginners this works only moderately: the model titles are proper engineering names (e.g. 'Four-bar Linkage', 'Verge and Foliot Escapement') with no plain-English grouping by what the mechanism does for you
coverage.scope_match: medium. It is entirely about mechanism TYPES, with good in-scope families (ratchets and pawls, Geneva/indexing, escapements, planetary trains, universal joints, couplings and clutches, belt drives). But it is limited to about 220 historic teaching models, and has nothing on snap fits, compliant or print-in-place joints, everyday quick-release hardware, powered connectors or adhesives
coverage.taxonomy_used: Reuleaux's kinematic classification as used in Gustav Voigt's model catalogue. It has about 25 lettered classes (A-Z, no J), with titles translated here from the German: A lower pairs; B higher pairs; C simple kinematic chains for inversion; D crank mechanisms; E crank mechanisms with pin expansion; F crank chamber mechanisms; G compound gear trains; H auxiliary apparatus; I chamber wheels (rotary pumps); K angled slotted-link chains; L cam/curve-driven sliding; M screws; N ratchet and indexing gear (Sperr- und Schaltwerke); O planetary gear trains; P jointed couplings (universal joints); Q gear teeth; R spherical cycloids; S straight-line mechanisms; T parallel guides; U position guides; V belt drives; W friction wheels; X clock escapements; Y reversing and change gears; Z couplings/clutches. The class list is from DMG-Lib's copy of the Voigt catalogue; that Cornell uses the same codes is reported in search snippets [uncertain]
coverage.example_types: Geneva (Maltese-cross) indexing drive (N8); star-wheel indexing drive (N9); ratchet with inner and outer pawls (N1); centrifugal ratchet (N2); silent ratchet (N3); clamping (friction) ratchet, i.e. roller-type freewheel (N4-N6); Chubb, Yale and Bramah lock mechanisms (N13-N15); power escapement (N25); planetary gear train (O1-O5); Hooke's universal joint and double universal joint (P1, P2); Oldham cross coupling (Z5); cone clutch (Z7); reversing gear with friction clutch (Y19); fast-and-loose pulley belt drive (V1); friction wheels (W series); verge and foliot escapement (X1); Graham anchor escapement (X7); differential screw (M7); screw chain with automatic release (M4); worm, i.e. 'endless screw' (C9); Reuleaux triangle in a square (curve of constant width, B2). The class codes are from the Voigt catalogue; not every one is confirmed to be among Cornell's surviving models [uncertain]
coverage.making_methods: General engineering education and the history of machines. There is also an early 3D-printing (rapid prototyping) strand: Lipson and Moon printed working, pre-assembled replicas of Reuleaux models on a Stratasys FDM machine in ABS with soluble support, and the STL files were offered for download
coverage.item_count: About 220 Reuleaux models (Voigt catalogue) at Cornell per Lipson et al.; ASME counts 230 Reuleaux models among about 300 artifacts; 58 items in the eCommons KMODDL References collection. The number of Digital Collections records could not be checked [uncertain]
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: torque-limiting: only indirectly (friction clutches and couplings in the Y and Z classes, not safety slip clutches); self-locking: partly (screw mechanisms, clamping/friction ratchets); hand-release only: no explicit coverage; one-way/ratchet: yes (the N class: tooth ratchets, silent ratchets, clamping ratchets, centrifugal ratchets); indexing/detent: yes (Geneva and star-wheel indexing, escapements); over-centre: no explicit coverage; compliant: no; print-in-place: indirectly (the project printed pre-assembled working replicas in one piece using soluble support, an early form of print-in-place); gear trains/gearboxes: yes (compound, planetary and reversing gear trains, gear-tooth forms, worm); powered connectors: no; adhesive types: no
coverage.entry_structure: Per model: title (proper name), model code, photos (often several angles), and for some an animated GIF or movie; a systematic description, maker (Gustav Voigt Werkstatt, Berlin), date and subject terms; in the original site, also historical and mathematical notes, links to relevant pages in digitised historic books, simulations, and for a few models an STL file. No design rules, degrees-of-freedom data or how-to [uncertain]
coverage.audience_level: school (middle and high school tutorials) / undergraduate / research and history of technology; not aimed at makers

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: medium. The clear photos and moving GIFs of real brass-and-iron models are very approachable, and tutorials were written for school level. But titles use 19th-century engineering names, there is no plain-English 'what is it for' grouping, and the original tutorials and simulations only survive on a partly broken archived site
usefulness.has_images: yes. High-quality studio photographs of every catalogued model (some by professional photographer Jon Reis), shot from several angles, and scans of historic book pages
usefulness.has_animations: yes. Animated GIFs for some models (a canned search on Digital Collections), movies of the models in motion, and, on the original site, interactive simulations of the maths behind the motions [uncertain: whether the simulations still run]
usefulness.gaps: Only about 220 historic teaching models, so many modern and maker-relevant types are missing (snap fits, living hinges, compliant and print-in-place joints, heat-set inserts, quick-release pins, cam buckles, torque limiters, electromagnetic latches, adhesives); no design rules or dimensions; no plain-English grouping; much of the original interactive content (tutorials, simulations, STL downloads) is now only on a partly broken archive; content is split across three platforms, and the Digital Collections portal blocks automated access
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: medium. Digital Collections items have per-item catalog URLs (of the form digital.library.cornell.edu/catalog/ss:<id>, seen in search results but not opened here) [uncertain], and eCommons texts have stable Handle URLs, e.g. https://ecommons.cornell.edu/handle/1813/57656 for the collection. The per-model pages on the original kmoddl.library.cornell.edu site are no longer live (archived only)
usefulness.reusable_data: Partly structured. eCommons is a DSpace repository with a working public JSON REST API (checked: https://ecommons.cornell.edu/server/api/pid/find?id=1813/57656 returns the collection record, and its discover/search endpoint returns item lists). The KMODDL metadata was designed with controlled vocabularies and shared through OAI-PMH with the NSDL (per D-Lib 2005). Digital Collections metadata may be exportable, but could not be checked because of the bot-check [uncertain]. No licence is stated for reusing the list itself. The model list (Voigt codes and names) is historical and effectively a public-domain catalogue
usefulness.maintained: Partly. The landing page on the Cornell Engineering Library site is live (2026) and links to Digital Collections and eCommons. The original 2003 site is archived on Archive-It, and the library itself warns that 'not all resources or navigation are functional' there. No active development has been seen since the 2002-2006 grants [uncertain]
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: (1) Use the Reuleaux/Voigt class letters as an optional 'family' index next to plain-English names. (2) Pair each mechanism type with a short looping animated GIF: cheap, works everywhere, and very beginner-friendly. (3) Offer downloadable 3D-printable replicas (STL) of classic mechanisms, printed pre-assembled, so makers can hold and try each type. The Lipson/Moon paper shows ratchets, escapements, slider-cranks and straight-line linkages printed as working assemblies. (4) Link each type to the historic book page where it first appears, to give provenance. (5) Write tutorials at several levels (middle school, high school, undergraduate) for the same model
usefulness.design_rules_given: No. The paper '3D-Printing the History of Mechanisms' discusses printing replicas (FDM, ABS, soluble support between moving parts) qualitatively, but gives no clearance numbers in the parts read [uncertain]
usefulness.generator_or_parametric: No generator. Fixed STL files of a few CAD-modelled Reuleaux models were made for download (not parametric)
usefulness.file_formats: JPEG/TIFF photos, animated GIFs, video (format not confirmed), PDFs of digitised books and papers (eCommons), and STL files for 3D-printing replicas (original site; whether they are still downloadable is unconfirmed) [uncertain]
usefulness.terminology_value: medium. It is authoritative for classic English and 19th-century German names of mechanism types (via Voigt/Reuleaux: e.g. 'Kreuzkupplung von Oldham' = Oldham coupling, 'Klemmsperrung' = clamping ratchet), and useful for historical aliases. It does not cover modern or maker vocabulary
usefulness.decision_support: None. There is no selector, flow chart or comparison. It offers only faceted search and browse in Digital Collections and a canned search for animated GIFs
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: Built on Cornell's physical Reuleaux collection (bought by Andrew D. White in 1882) and Gustav Voigt's 1907 catalogue of Reuleaux models, with Reuleaux's 'Kinematics of Machinery' as the theory behind it. It overlaps heavily with DMG-Lib, which also holds Reuleaux models (e.g. at Hannover), reproduces the Voigt catalogue class list, and links to KMODDL on its 'Mechanisms worldwide' page. It also overlaps with 507 Mechanical Movements-style collections for the classic linkages. A planned second collection (Boston Museum of Science's Clark Collection of Mechanical Movements) was announced in 2005, but it could not be confirmed that it was added [uncertain]
